notes.h: What special needs means (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A family member has special needs when they need support beyond the usual family routine. The needs can be physical, mental or emotional, and the family's response depends on which kind it is.
points: Physical needs include limited mobility, sensory impairment (loss of sight or hearing) and long-term illness, so the member may need help with movement, personal care or equipment.
Mental needs include intellectual disability, learning disability, autism and mental health difficulties, so the member may need extra help with learning, communication or daily decisions.
Emotional needs include behavioural or emotional difficulties, so the member may need patient, consistent support from the whole family.
Special needs can be present from birth or acquired later through accident, illness or age, so any family can find itself in this situation.
The member can be a child, an adult or an older relative, so a family may be a parent caring for a child or adult children caring for a parent.
Use respectful language: talk about a member with special needs, and focus on the person and their abilities, not just the condition.
notes.tip: The exam asks about 'a member' of the family, not only a child, so write answers that work for parents of a child as well as for an adult or older relative.

notes.h: How the family responds to a member with special needs (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The family responds practically, emotionally and financially, and usually draws on outside services as well. A good answer covers several of these, each with its purpose.
points: Care at home: family members provide daily personal care, supervision and transport, often reorganising work and routines around the member's needs.
Adapting the home: ramps, wider doorways, grab rails, a downstairs bedroom and special equipment improve access and safety, so the member can move around the house with less help.
Encouraging independence: the family builds the member's skills in self-care, communication, mobility and decision-making, within safe limits, and helps the member to integrate into the community.
Working with professionals and organisations: doctors, therapists, teachers and social workers plan support together with the family, so that care is coordinated.

Claiming assistance: families apply for all the State assistance and grants the member qualifies for, including income support and those for equipment and adaptations, because the costs of care are high.
Emotional support: family members reassure the member, listen to concerns and protect the member's dignity and self-worth, treating the member as a full member of the family.
Siblings also need attention, so that they do not feel overlooked while the family focuses on the member with special needs.
Advocacy: families speak up for the member's rights and lobby (campaign) for better services and State support.
notes.tip: When asked how a family might respond, cover home care, adapting the home, independence, professionals and organisations, claiming grants, emotional and financial support, and lobbying, giving the reason for each.

notes.h: Difficulties the family may experience (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Caring for a member with special needs can put pressure on a family's time, money, health and relationships. Marking schemes credit development, so for each difficulty state the problem and then its effect.
points: Limited employment and educational opportunities for the member restrict independence and income.
Social isolation and prejudice exclude the member and the family from community life, so they may have fewer friends and less support.
A shortage of help and respite (a short break from caring) leaves carers exhausted.
Limited mobility and inaccessible transport and buildings restrict daily life, so even simple outings need planning.
Stress, fatigue and fear for the future, particularly about who will care for the member when parents can no longer do so.
notes.tip: For 'challenges', give the problem and then its consequence, for example a parent giving up work leading to loss of income and strain on the budget. A bare list earns less than a developed point.

notes.h: Difficulties with services, money and family life (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Gaps in services and the cost of care also affect the household budget and the relationships within the family.
points: Inadequate State financial support can force a parent to give up paid work to provide full-time care, which means a loss of income.
Insufficient medical, therapy and educational services cause delays in assessment and support, so the member may go without help they need.
The extra costs of care, equipment and transport place strain on the household budget, especially when income has fallen.
Siblings may be given added duties and receive less parental attention, which can strain relationships.
Challenging behaviour in some conditions strains relationships and daily routines.

notes.b: Statutory services are provided or funded by the State. They are a family's first source of professional help and financial support.
points: Health, disability and social care services come mainly through the HSE, which offers health, disability and family support services, including physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, public health nurses, respite and day services, and assessment of need.
The Disability Act 2005 gives the right to an assessment of health and education needs and to a service statement, and families can request this assessment in order to access services.
Education services for children with special educational needs are provided through schools within the State education system, using resource teaching and special needs assistants.

The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) coordinates these supports, under the Education for All Children with Special Educational Needs Act 2004 (the EPSEN Act), the Act on the educational needs of children with special needs.
Social welfare supports include Domiciliary Care Allowance for a child with a severe disability, Disability Allowance for adults, and Carer's Allowance for the person providing care.
The Carer's Support Grant is a yearly payment to carers that may fund respite, giving the carer a break.
A medical card is available for those who qualify, and housing adaptation grants through the local authority help pay for changes such as ramps.
notes.tip: For 'statutory versus voluntary', give examples of each and say what each offers. Remember that statutory means provided by the State, so never call a charity statutory.

notes.b: Voluntary organisations are independent, non-profit bodies. They work alongside the State rather than replacing it, and they are funded partly by the State and partly by fundraising and donations.
points: They provide services, support and advocacy, including respite care, support groups, training, advocacy and information, which statutory services may not provide.
The Rehab Group is a non-profit organisation with service areas: education, training, employment, social care and home services, all to promote equality for people with disabilities.
The National Learning Network is the Rehab Group's training arm, offering training and qualifications for people with disabilities, and Rehab Enterprises provides employment.
Recycling projects and fundraising help to pay for the Rehab Group's work.
Enable Ireland provides services for children and adults with physical and neurological disability, and the Irish Wheelchair Association supports wheelchair users with housing and transport.
Down Syndrome Ireland supports people with Down syndrome and their families, Inclusion Ireland campaigns for people with intellectual disability, and AsIAm supports autistic people.
Voluntary services matter because they fill gaps in State provision, offer peer support from families in similar situations, and campaign for rights.
notes.tip: For 'voluntary organisation', name it first, then say who it serves, its services, how it is funded and its aim of equality. The Rehab Group is the usual example.

notes.h: Investigation: how one family might respond (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The syllabus suggests a short case study of a family with a member who has a physical disability, to show how a family uses both statutory and voluntary services.
points: Choose a family, real with permission or an imagined example clearly labelled as such, and describe the member's needs without medical detail.
Describe how the family responds: care at home, adapting the home, encouraging independence and emotional support.
List the statutory services the family uses, such as the HSE, school supports and social welfare payments, and what each provides.
List the voluntary organisations the family uses and what each offers, such as respite, peer support or training.
Finish with the difficulties the family faces and how services help, because this ties the response to the challenges.

keyTerms.definition: Physical, mental or emotional needs that require support beyond what the usual family routine can provide.
A service the State is responsible for providing, funded through public money and delivered under official responsibility.
An independent, non-profit body that provides services, support or advocacy, usually relying on donations, fundraising and volunteers.
Temporary relief for a full-time carer, in which another person looks after the person in need of care for a short period.
Speaking up for and defending the rights and interests of a person who may find it hard to do so alone.
Equipment that helps a person with a disability carry out everyday tasks, such as a wheelchair or a hoist.
A person, often a family member, who provides regular unpaid care to a relative with ongoing needs.
A lack of contact with family, friends and the community, which can affect a person's health and wellbeing.

factCards.term: Three difficulties a family may face when a member has special needs
factCards.definition: Limited employment and educational opportunities; social isolation and prejudice; and loss of income with extra costs.

factCards.term: Four ways a family can respond to a member with a disability
factCards.definition: Providing care at home; adapting the home; encouraging independence; and claiming all available assistance and grants.

factCards.term: Three sources of help from outside the family
factCards.definition: Statutory services, voluntary organisations, and professionals such as therapists and teachers.

factCards.term: Five service areas of the Rehab Group
factCards.definition: Education, training, employment, social care and home services for people with disabilities.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways a family can adapt its home and routines to meet the needs of a member with special needs.
questions.model: Any three, each with a brief explanation. Ramps, wider doorways and grab rails make the home accessible. A downstairs bedroom removes the need for stairs. Routines are reorganised around the member's care, for example by arranging work hours, transport and daily supervision. Encouraging the member to learn self-care within safe limits builds independence.

questions.prompt: Discuss the difficulties a family may experience when a member has special needs, and explain how statutory services and voluntary organisations can help.
questions.model: Difficulties: limited employment and educational opportunities for the member; social isolation and prejudice; shortage of help and respite, leaving carers exhausted; limited mobility and inaccessible transport; inadequate State financial support, which can force a parent out of paid work; insufficient medical and educational services; loss of income and extra costs; added duties for siblings; stress and fear for the future. Statutory services: the HSE provides health, disability and family support services, the education system provides support for children with special educational needs, and a formal assessment of needs allows access to these services. Voluntary organisations: independent, non-profit bodies such as the Rehab Group offer education, training, employment, social care and home services, and can provide respite care, support groups and advocacy. Full marks need several difficulties explained, at least one statutory and one voluntary service with its role, and a link between the service and the difficulty it addresses.
